code.title: Sync vs async execution order

followUps:
Because 0 is only a minimum wait: the callback goes into the timer queue and can run only after the current code and all pending microtasks finish. The call stack must be empty first.

Example: setTimeout(f, 0); while (Date.now() < end) {} with a 50 ms loop runs f after about 50 ms, not at 0. Browsers also clamp nested timers to about 4 ms. Use queueMicrotask or a promise if you need to run right after the current code.

Split the work so the thread gets breathing room, or move it off the main thread. Short answer: chunk it, or use a worker.

  1. Chunk: process 1,000 items, then yield with setTimeout(next, 0) or requestIdleCallback, so clicks and rendering can run between chunks.
  2. Worker: send data to a Web Worker (browser) or worker_threads (Node) and receive the result as a message.
  3. Algorithm: do less work (cache, debounce, virtualise lists).

Example: 1,000,000 items in chunks of 10,000 gives 100 short tasks instead of one long freeze.

code.title: Callback hell vs a flat promise chain

followUps:
Inversion of control means you hand your code to someone else's function and trust them to call it correctly, instead of controlling the flow yourself. With a callback, the other function decides when, how often and in what way it runs.

Risks: it might call your callback twice (charging a card twice), never, too early, or with a swallowed error. A promise reverses this: the library returns an object and you decide what to do with it, and a promise settles only once.

"Releasing Zalgo" means an API that calls your callback synchronously sometimes and asynchronously other times, so callers cannot predict the order. The fix: always be async (or always sync).

Example: a cache lookup calls cb(value) immediately on a hit, but after I/O on a miss. Code after the call then runs before the callback on a miss but after it on a hit, causing bugs. Fix with process.nextTick(() => cb(value)) or queueMicrotask so it is always async. Promises .then handlers are always async, which avoids this.

code.title: Promise states and settling once

followUps:
No, there is no standard way to read a promise's state synchronously; you can only react to it with .then, .catch or await, which run later. This is on purpose, so code behaves the same whether the value was ready already or not.

Workaround: race it against a marker, e.g. Promise.race([p, Symbol.for('pending')]) resolves to the marker if p is still pending, but even that answer arrives asynchronously. console.log(p) in Node shows the state only for debugging.

The promise rejects with a TypeError ("Chaining cycle detected"), because a promise cannot wait for itself forever.

Example: const p = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(p))); If it accepted p, it would follow its own result and never settle. The spec checks "is x the same promise?" first and rejects, as in the demo for question 9. Longer cycles (a waits for b, b waits for a) are not detected and hang pending forever.

code.title: promisify for error-first callbacks

followUps:
Implementing callbackify is the reverse of promisify: take a function that returns a promise and make it accept an error-first callback as the last argument.

const callbackify = (fn) => function (...args) {
  const cb = args.pop();
  fn.apply(this, args).then(
    (v) => process.nextTick(cb, null, v),
    (e) => process.nextTick(cb, e));
};

Use nextTick so an exception inside cb is not swallowed by the promise. A falsy rejection (like null) needs wrapping in an Error, because cb(null) would look like success.

Because a promise settles exactly once, but a data event fires many times, so you would only ever get the first chunk and lose the rest.

Example: a stream emits chunks 'a', 'b', 'c'. A promise made from the first data event resolves with 'a'; 'b' and 'c' are silently dropped. For repeated events use for await (const chunk of stream) (async iterators), or promisify only the one-time events like end via events.once(emitter, 'end').

code.title: What .then returns

followUps:
A promise handler is queued as a microtask, and returning a promise forces the engine to run an extra adoption job first, so it takes more ticks (about 3 instead of 1). The result is the same, just a little later.

Steps: the handler returns promise q; the engine schedules a job that calls q.then(resolveOuter) (one tick); that handler runs when q is fulfilled (another tick), and only then does the outer promise settle and its own handlers get queued. In the demo above, a chain of 3 plain thens finishes before one that returned a promise. It rarely matters, except when you rely on exact ordering.

Chaining makes one pipeline where b receives the result of a; branching makes two independent pipelines that both receive the original value of p.

Example: p fulfils with 1. Chain p.then(a).then(b) with a = x => x + 1 gives b the value 2. Branches p.then(a); p.then(b) give b the value 1, and an error in a is not seen by b (and becomes unhandled if nobody catches it). Branching is for fan-out; chaining is for sequences.

code.title: all, allSettled, race and any

followUps:
Here is the core: loop over the inputs, store results by index, count completions, and reject on the first failure.

function all(items) {
  return new Promise((res, rej) => {
    const out = []; let left = items.length;
    if (!left) return res(out);
    items.forEach((x, i) => Promise.resolve(x).then(
      (v) => { out[i] = v; if (--left === 0) res(out); }, rej));
  });
}

Key points: write to out[i] (not push) to keep input order, wrap with Promise.resolve to accept plain values, and handle the empty array. Extra rejections are ignored since the promise settled once.

You cannot cancel a promise, but you can tell the work to stop: give each task an AbortSignal and abort it once the race has a winner.

const ac = new AbortController();
const r = await Promise.any(
  urls.map((u) => fetch(u, { signal: ac.signal })));
ac.abort();   // stops the slower requests

With three mirrors, the first answer wins at 40 ms and aborting frees the other two sockets instead of letting them download for 300 ms more. Tasks that ignore signals cannot be stopped; their results are just discarded.

code.title: Error propagation in a chain

followUps:
Put catch at the end if you want one place that handles every step's failure; put it in the middle only when you can recover and let the chain continue.

Example: load().then(parse).then(save).catch(log) catches an error from any of the three. A middle catch like load().catch(() => defaults).then(parse) replaces a failure with default values, but it also hides the error for later steps, so use it only for errors you can really fix. A catch in the middle does not catch errors thrown after it unless another catch follows.

Wrap it with the cause option, so the new error carries the old one: throw new Error('load failed', { cause: err }). Then logs and callers can read e.cause for the original message and stack.

.catch((err) => {
  throw new Error('cannot load user ' + id, { cause: err });
});

Do not do throw new Error(err.message), which loses the stack and type. Do not return the error from catch either, because that turns the failure into a success value.

code.title: Sequential vs parallel tasks

followUps:
A function that returns a promise is a task you can start later; a promise is a task that already started. Sequential execution needs to control when each task starts, and a promise gives you no such control.

Example: [fetchA(), fetchB()] has already launched both requests, so awaiting them one by one is still parallel. [fetchA, fetchB] lets you call fetchB only after fetchA finished. Sequence time is the sum (30 + 10 = 40 ms), parallel is the maximum (30 ms).

mapLimit runs at most limit tasks at the same time and keeps results in input order. The demo above shows a worker-based version. Steps:

  1. Make limit workers sharing one index counter.
  2. Each worker loops: take the next index, await fn(item), store at that index.
  3. Wait for all workers with Promise.all.
let next = 0;
const worker = async () => {
  while (next < items.length) { const i = next++; out[i] = await fn(items[i]); }
};

Time is about N / limit times the task time; memory is O(N) for the results.

code.title: Unhandled rejections

followUps:
Because the rejection is reported when the microtask queue drains after the rejection happens, and a timer callback runs later, so the report has already been made. Attaching .catch inside setTimeout is too late.

Example: const p = Promise.reject(e); setTimeout(() => p.catch(h), 0); triggers unhandledRejection first (and in Node 15+ the process crashes) and the handler later only produces a "handled asynchronously" warning. Attach handlers in the same tick the promise is created or returned.

The second rejection is ignored by Promise.all, because the combined promise already rejected with the first one. It will not crash your program, since Promise.all attached handlers to every input promise.

Example: Promise.all([failAt(5), failAt(10)]) rejects with the 5 ms error. The 10 ms error is silently dropped, so you may lose information. If you need every error, use Promise.allSettled or Promise.any (which collects them in an AggregateError).

code.title: Thenable adoption and resolution

followUps:
For a native promise p, Promise.resolve(p) returns the very same object p, with no wrapping and no extra tick. This is the check Promise.resolve(p) === p in the demo.

It applies only when p.constructor is the same Promise constructor. For a thenable that is not a real promise, or a promise from a subclass, you get a new promise that adopts it. This is why Promise.resolve(x) is a safe way to normalise a value that might or might not be a promise.

Reading then twice could give different answers, because it may be a getter, so the spec reads it once and keeps that function. This stops a hostile or buggy object from changing behaviour between the check and the call.

Example: a getter returns a function the first time and undefined the second. If the engine checked "is it callable?" and then read it again, it could crash or call undefined. Reading once, then calling that saved reference, is safe. The resolve and reject functions are also once-guarded: only the first call counts.

code.title: Timeout and cancel with race and AbortSignal

followUps:
Merge them with AbortSignal.any: it returns one signal that aborts as soon as any input signal aborts, and its reason says which one.

const user = new AbortController();
const signal = AbortSignal.any([
  user.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000)]);
fetch(url, { signal });

If the user clicks cancel at 2 s, the reason is the user's reason; if nothing happens, at 5 s you get a TimeoutError. For older runtimes, create one controller and call abort() from both a timer and the user handler.

A per-attempt timeout limits one try; a deadline limits the whole operation including all retries and waits. Use both.

Example: 4 attempts each with a 2 s timeout and delays of 1, 2 and 4 s could take 8 + 7 = 15 s in the worst case. With a total deadline of 10 s, the retry loop stops starting new attempts once the remaining time is too small. Without a deadline, a caller waiting 15 s may have already given up while your retries keep consuming resources.

code.title: Retry with backoff and jitter

followUps:
Jitter adds randomness to the wait so that many clients do not retry at the same moment, which would hit a recovering server with a wave of requests (the thundering herd).

Example: 1,000 clients fail together and all wait exactly 2 s, so 1,000 requests arrive in the same instant again. With full jitter, each waits a random time between 0 and 2 s, so about 500 requests per second spread out over that range. Without jitter, exponential backoff only delays the stampede; it does not spread it.

Send the same unique idempotency key with every attempt of one logical request; the server stores the first result under that key and returns it again for repeats, so a retry cannot create a second charge.

const key = crypto.randomUUID(); // once per operation
retry(() => fetch(url, { method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': key }, body }));

Create the key before the first attempt, not inside the retry loop. Server side: keep a table of key to response for a day or so. Without it, a timeout where the server did process the request gets retried and processed twice.

code.title: Unbounded Promise.all vs mapLimit

followUps:
Carry a trace id with every request and every async hop, and record a span (start and end time) for each step. In Node, AsyncLocalStorage keeps the id attached across await and callbacks without passing it by hand.

  1. Generate or read a traceparent header at the edge.
  2. Store it in AsyncLocalStorage.
  3. Copy it into outgoing HTTP calls, queue messages and logs.

OpenTelemetry does this automatically. Then one id shows that a 900 ms request spent 700 ms in one slow downstream call.

Measure queue depth, running count, wait time, run time and failures, because those show whether the pool is too small, too big or the downstream is unhealthy.

  • Active tasks versus limit (is the pool saturated?).
  • Queue length and time spent waiting in the queue.
  • Task duration percentiles (p50, p95, p99).
  • Success, error and timeout counts, retries.

Example: limit 10, queue length growing from 0 to 5,000 while p95 duration doubles means the downstream is slowing down; alert on that instead of just raising the limit.

code.title: Cancellation with AbortController

followUps:
Pass the signal into mapLimit and check it before starting every new task and again when each task ends, then pass the same signal to each task so running ones stop too.

async function worker() {
  while (next < items.length) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    const i = next++;
    out[i] = await fn(items[i], signal);
  }
}

When the signal aborts, no new items start, running tasks reject with the abort reason, and Promise.all rejects with it. With 1,000 items and limit 5, an abort at item 40 leaves 955 items untouched.

The finally step should run, release resources and then let the abort error continue; it must not swallow it or replace it with a normal result.

try {
  await work(signal);
} finally {
  conn.release();   // always runs, even on abort
}

Do not return from finally, because that hides the rejection. Treat AbortError as an expected outcome rather than a failure: do not log it as an error, do not retry it, and do not count it in error metrics.
